ai-b0760b4eff.headline: Quarter of India’s labour force highly exposed to AI, says report
ai-b0760b4eff.fulltext:
In one of the first such studies of the impact on AI on Indian workforce using India’s own labour data, a new report finds that nearly a quarter of the country’s labour force is engaged in work that is ‘highly exposed’ to AI.
The analysis from the Centre for Finance and Economic Research, Great Lakes Institute of Management took into account data from the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS).
The higher exposure to AI can have both complementary and substitution effects depending on the job profile with 7.6 per cent of the workforce expected to see increased productivity, while 11.4 per cent may face substitution risk.
However, in a plus, occupations such as agriculture as well as skilled trades — who together account for 54.4 per cent of India’s workforce — face relatively low substitution risk — both from AI or conventional machine driven automation.
The report is authored by Vidya Mahambare, Vivek Jadhav, and Vishnu Venugopalan.
Unveiling the report at an event here on Sunday, V Anantha Nageswaran Chief Economic Advisor, Government of India noted that the task before policymakers is to improve the quality of existing exposure through AI literacy, task redesign, and reskilling.
AI for productivity
Writing in the report’s foreword, the CEA said that employment in high-routine occupations that are susceptible to conventional automation and mechanisation regardless of what happens with AI, has risen by 4.8 percentage points since 2012. AI now competes for routine tasks, he said, stressing that the window to reskill and learn how to use AI for productivity is open.
Health, elderly care, education and the skilled trades, and other non-routine, high-complementarity occupations are areas where India needs more workers, he adds.
Meanwhile, the report mentioned that the share of people in occupations with more substitution risk is higher for younger employee cohorts — at 39.4 per cent in the 15–24 age group. In fact the 15-24 cohort have the worst ratio in terms of high-routine jobs to complementary jobs at 7.6 to 1 against roughly 4 to 1 for every older cohort.
As for the specific States, Maharashtra, Haryana, Kerala and Tamil Nadu have the highest shares of workers in AI-complementary occupations to build on.
As policy recommendations, the report suggested expanding AI literacy and reskilling, particularly for young workers.
“Prioritise young, urban labour-market entrants, the unemployed and those in routine clerical, back-office and low-discretion technical roles for training in judgement, verification, and client engagement,” it said. Also target new AI-induced jobs such as data annotators and AI trainers, it noted, among other recommendations.
Published on October 11, 2026

global-economics-4fb71c5c6d.headline: India's Central Bank Deploys Sweeping Measures to Halt Rupee's Record Slide
global-economics-4fb71c5c6d.fulltext:
India's Central Bank Deploys Sweeping Measures to Halt Rupee's Record Slide
India's monetary authority has unveiled its most aggressive intervention in the foreign-exchange market since the 2013 currency crisis, rolling out a package of measures designed to break the rupee's relentless decline after it touched a record low against the dollar.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announced the steps on Saturday, pairing a dedicated dollar facility for the country's three state-run oil refiners with a new reserve requirement that will force lenders to park cash with the central bank on certain currency derivative transactions.
The rupee, Asia's worst-performing major currency this year, closed last Friday at 96.7350 per dollar, barely above the all-time low of 96.9650 recorded in May. It has shed more than 7% against the greenback in 2026 despite two rate hikes, heavy dollar-selling by the central bank, and a diaspora deposit program that pulled in US$133 billion. The RBI's foreign-currency reserves contracted by US$51 billion in the four weeks through Oct. 2 as policymakers fought to slow the slide.
Under the new arrangement, Indian Oil Corp, Bharat Petroleum Corp, and Hindustan Petroleum Corp will be able to purchase dollars directly from the central bank's reserves through designated lenders rather than tapping the open market. The facility became operational on Monday. The central bank took a similar step in 2013, when it opened a dollar window for oil companies and provided roughly US$12 billion to refiners during the taper-tantrum episode.
The fresh package also introduces an entirely new tool: a foreign-exchange risk reserve. Lenders will be required to hold with the RBI the rupee equivalent of 20% of the notional amount of any derivative transaction exceeding US$2 million. Other regulatory changes prohibit dealers from re-booking canceled foreign-exchange derivatives involving the rupee and slash the limit for derivative trades without an established underlying exposure to US$5 million from US$100 million.
"The RBI's measures represent a virtual shutdown of the market," said Anil Kumar Bhansali, head of treasury at Finrex Treasury Advisors in Mumbai. "The dollar demand from hedging and from the oil companies will now exit the market plus there are severe restrictions on export and import activities. We should see at least a 1% rally in the rupee on Monday."
The offshore market reacted immediately, with the currency strengthening 0.6% in New York after the announcement.
Anindya Banerjee, head of research for commodity and currency derivatives at Kotak Neo, described the package as "the most comprehensive set of currency-market measures since 2013."
Yet economists cautioned that the intervention addresses symptoms rather than underlying imbalances. Foreign investors have pulled more than US$30 billion from Indian equities this year amid a rotation toward artificial-intelligence-linked markets, while elevated crude prices continue to inflate the import bill.
"This is a short-term fix, not a structural solution," said Radhika Piplani, economist at Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd. "High crude prices, capital outflows and underlying dollar demand remain key risks. The measures may buy the RBI time, but a sustained rupee recovery will require an improvement in these fundamentals."
The central bank has been cycling through policy tools in recent months. Earlier this year it capped daily net open positions for banks at US$100 million and banned lenders from offering non-deliverable rupee contracts to clients, only to roll back the latter restriction. In June, the government removed taxes on foreign bond investments and launched the diaspora deposit scheme that raised US$133 billion.
The direct dollar sales to refiners carry a trade-off: while they remove substantial demand from the spot market, they also draw down reserves that have already fallen sharply. That tension will likely shape how long the RBI can sustain the program if outflows persist.
For now, traders expect a relief rally when onshore markets reopen. Whether it endures will depend on the trajectory of global energy prices, the pace of foreign outflows, and the central bank's willingness to keep tightening liquidity in the currency market.

ai-c8e6c94077.headline: Is AI Crowding Everyone Else Out of the Bond Market?
ai-c8e6c94077.fulltext:
[Text below is Yahoo Finance's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Hyperscalers, data centers and chip companies are borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to finance the AI buildout, turning the technology boom into one of the biggest new forces in corporate credit. Investors are still buying, but rising concentration, complex data-center financing and competition with government borrowing are raising a harder question: how much AI debt can the market absorb?
This is a story about trees growing to the sky. They say it doesn't happen, but looking at the investment in AI, you have to wonder whether this just might be the exception. It's already historic and looks only to keep growing. But where is all that money coming from? And can it pay off for investors?
I see through 2027, at least $1 trillion.
In fact, we are going to be short. I am certain computing demand will be much higher than that.
By now, we all know that AI has an insatiable appetite for compute, and that means more data centers, chips, and other expensive infrastructure. Equity investors have already benefited seeing shares of the six hyperscalers rise by an average of 15% year to date. Now, it's the debt investor's turn.
So the numbers keep growing. Um, and I think that's the challenging piece of it.
Debt investors like Lauren Moran, a fixed income portfolio manager at Wellington Management.
When we look back to 2025, where really this borrowing from hyperscalers had really only begun. Um, through the course of 2026, we're probably looking at around 300 billion in the investment grade, um market borrowings from hyperscalers themselves.
By some estimates, the tech sector accounted for just 5% of investment grade corporate bond issuance in 2024. That number is now close to 20%.
When we think about over the course of this year, likely we'll see two and a quarter trillion of total issuance in the US investment grade market. So it's a pretty substantial portion of the debt that we're seeing in the market. And importantly, when we think about the actual growth in our debt markets is largely coming from the hyperscalers at this point. and we look at year over year investment grade issuance being up around 35%.
So far, what's the appetite for all this debt? And and to make it a little simpler, let's start with investment grade for the hyperscalers. So there's other financing, but just start with that. It seems like there's a fair appetite for that debt.
Yeah, it certainly started off with a huge amount of appetite. These were new issuers, they were double A rated balance sheets. People were very excited to be able to actually buy this debt in the market. I'd say every subsequent deal in every global market, that's starting to shift. Um, buyers are demanding more compensation to lend to these issuers as there are growing footprint in our markets. The other component is is there's just an overall demand for capital from sovereign balance sheets globally as well.
Also a fair amount of M&A activity too. And so we're just seeing a little bit of stress in terms of just the sheer size uh in demand for capital globally, um that's causing more indigestion.
They have had, I don't want to say infinite capacity, but more than enough capacity to do what they need. The real question will be as we get into next year, does that sustain?
Scott Schulte is the global co-head of investment grade debt syndicate at Barclays.
I wonder about how you analyze the risk associated with AI debt, and one of them is what you just suggested. Is there a concentration risk apart from the index in terms of the equities, just in terms of the debt, is there a concentration risk when you get that much debt against that particular application?
Right now, the big five hyperscalers are about 5% of the index. But again, go back two or three years, that was 1 to 2%. So that concentration has jumped up meaningfully. Now they're still 95% of the index of other things. But they are now actually becoming some of the leading components. And so whereas banks used to be the top of the index, JP Morgan, Bank of America, because obviously perpetual funding needs, they tend to issue much shorter debt.
Hyperscalers prefer much longer debt because it fits the business model much better. And so as you think about what we call the duration of the index, it's extending meaningfully because they issue 20, 30, 40, 100-year debt in some instances.
Moran says we've seen the risks of concentration before.
Harkening back to, you know, when we think about post GFC and thinking about money center bank concentration, which typically has been the largest source of concentration risk in the market that we've dealt with, the AI hyperscalar trade will easily overtake the US Money Center banks in terms of concentration over the course of the next, you know, year and a half or two years.
Hyperscalers are flooding debt markets with more than just traditional corporate bonds. Special purpose vehicles allow them to issue bonds specifically for data centers, keeping the debt off their balance sheets.
The investment grade markets, as I mentioned, are actually being asked to bear a lot of different types of risk than we do traditionally. So the hyperscalers may actually get to a point where they're very attractive, um incremental bond market market opportunities, whereas data centers are a little bit different. And I think the nuance there is data center financing bears much different risk profiles than we typically have in the investment grade market. You have construction risk, you have permitting risk, you have electrification risk. And so this ultimately is being born by a market that this is very new to.
I think where you're seeing more differentiation is in some of the off-balance sheet structures, whether it's the GPU financings, the chip financings, the actual data centers themselves. Uh you've seen in recent days there's been force majeure, uh at least implied in a couple of instances. And so you have to start thinking about the AI ecosystem holistically and tangentially what impacts it, meaning, can I get the power? Can I get the transmission? Can I get the heating and cooling? Can I get the thing built in two years when it's supposed to be built? And if it's not, what are the outs that the hyperscalar might have in terms of the contractual agreement on that data center?
It's the hyperscalers issuing much of the debt, but not all hyperscalers are created equal as they go into fixed income markets.
You see actually a a fair amount of dispersion within the sector, both in terms of absolute levels, but also in terms of how the market um treats their credit curves as well. I'd say a big piece of that has actually been governance, clarity around financial policy, um and otherwise, you know, what credit investors typically want is certainty of cash flows, very clear expectations around financial policy, prudence. Um and that is more challenging. This is a sector that historically has not had a lot of debt, but we are seeing the market differentiate between more levered balance sheets, highly levered balance sheets, like an Oracle versus less levered balance sheets like a Microsoft. And so it is not all one trade, but you do have an underlying theme that they tend to move with some correlation to to one another, but with slightly different betas.
Subadra Rajappa is the head of Americas Research at Societe Generale. And though she sees investors paying attention to the health of borrower's balance sheets, she says there's still a market for riskier hyperscalar debt, if the price is right.
There are some names that are that are uh trading at a at a significant discount. The markets are getting more and more sensitive. I mean just in the last couple of weeks, we've seen a significant amount of widening in in some of the high yield names. So the investors are getting more and more discerning. The general level of yields have have gone up quite substantially and corporate bond spreads are still relatively healthy. So for the investor, it's a it's a question of all in yield. and the all in yield is still quite attractive in some of these names.
But with so much debt being taken up with AI, what does that leave for the rest? Those needing capital for things other than AI infrastructure, especially when yields overall have been steadily rising for all borrowers.
Well, talking about those spreads or those yields, is there a noticeable difference between on the one hand, AI borrowing and other corporate investment grade?
AI borrowing is is quite a lot. It might be crowding out some of the other investors who are coming into the market. Um, but it really depends on what type of investor you're talking about. Some of the the corporates that are trying to come to the market can wait for a little bit longer and issue next year. They're trying to evaluate the general level of yields right now and figure out if the opportunity is a right for them. But, you know, the hyperscalers have their mandate. They're going to be issuing a lot this year, more to come next year, and they're a little bit, you know, I would say time agnostic if you will.
There are risks associated with AI, um execution risk, uh variety of sorts, whether it's power, or it's resistance, community resistance. Uh also concentration risk because there's just so much of it. Is that being reflected in the bond market so far for AI?
Uh that's a very good question, David, because I think that it's really hard to to see that in the data as of yet. Like I just mentioned, I mean, the the uh some of the high yield names are starting to come under pressure. You are seeing investors being a little bit more discerning about where they put their money to work. But as of now, I think that the that the supply is being very well absorbed.
It's not just AI debt that looks like it's growing to the sky. AI companies are right alongside other corporate borrowers in competing with sovereign issuers as governments around the world contend with debt burdens that just keep growing higher with the inevitable move to higher yields.
So the the broader dynamic is at play here for me still, even though we're talking about hyperscalers and the issuance that's coming out of the the corporate bond sector, is is the magnitude of the debt and deficits in developed markets. So it's this is not just a US phenomena, you're seeing a lot more uh of that happening globally, whether it be Japan or the UK, more issuance coming from uh the uh likes of Germany, um for defense spending or infrastructure as well as uh you know, some of the spreads that we've seen in in countries like France that are starting to widen out. So government bond debt in general, um you know, for the for the longest time has been uh a source of of demand for for investors. and now you're seeing this this competition for capital if you will. So, investors now have the option of either investing in government bonds or corporate bond bonds at higher yields, but broadly speaking, my perspective is that government bonds are starting to crowd out the the larger uh you know, bond market complex.
Investors haven't found the ceiling for the debt binge yet, but unless these trees truly do grow to the sky, there is a ceiling up there somewhere. And when we reach it, the consequences may extend well beyond the bond market.
I think that my concern broadly speaking is all the issues that you just raised with what happens to this investment? How does that, you know, do these larger companies recoup some of their capex that they're spending uh in in in AI for for not just this year but but for the next several years. And, you know, there's there's also as we head into the midterms, I'm a little bit concerned about um, you know, what the pushback might be for data center uh development, would that slow down the progress on AI?

indian-startups-c4dab54043.headline: Zetwerk raises fresh issue size to Rs 2,830 Cr, OFS component up 49% in RHP
indian-startups-c4dab54043.fulltext:
Manufacturing platform Zetwerk has filed its Red Herring Prospectus (RHP) for its initial public offering (IPO), comprising a fresh issue of shares worth Rs 2,830 crore.
According to its RHP, the Bengaluru-based company has increased its fresh issue size to Rs 2,830 crore from Rs 2,600 crore proposed in its updated draft red herring prospectus (UDRHP). The offer for sale (OFS) has also increased by 49% to 14.45 crore shares from 9.68 crore shares proposed in the UDRHP filed in August.
The OFS will include shares from promoters Amrit Pratik Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan, who will each sell 1.42 crore shares. Promoter group entity Creovate Innovation will offload up to 2.30 crore shares. Together, they will offer around 5.14 crore shares.
Among the existing investors, Lightspeed Venture Partners will offload the most, at 2.51 crore shares, followed by Peak XV Partners, which will sell 2.34 crore shares.
Kae Capital Fund and Kalysta Capital Fund will collectively sell up to 1.67 crore shares. Accel India V will also participate in the OFS, offloading up to 1.2 crore shares.
The offer will be open for subscription on October 15, 2026 to October 19, 2026 while anchor bid will start on October 14.
Zetwerk plans to use Rs 1,300 crore from the fresh issue to repay or prepay borrowings at the company level. Another Rs 860 crore will be used to repay debt at nine subsidiaries. The remaining proceeds will be allocated towards acquisitions, strategic investments and general corporate purposes.
Founded in 2017 by Acharya and Ramakkrushnan, Zetwerk operates a technology-led manufacturing platform that connects businesses with manufacturers and suppliers across sectors such as energy, electronics, aerospace, defence and industrial automation.
On the financial front, Zetwerk’s revenue from continuing operations rose to Rs 15,913 crore in FY26 from Rs 11,332 crore in FY25. In Q1 FY27, revenue from operations grew 55% year-on-year to Rs 4,118 crore, while losses from continuing operations declined 93% to Rs 64 crore from Rs 881 crore in the year-ago quarter.

world-a49756c40c.headline: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’
world-a49756c40c.fulltext:
Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.
In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.
He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.
Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.
Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure.
The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added.
The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.
Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.
The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.
The Financial Times, citing officials in Europe, reported on Sunday that the US is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.
On Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.
Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.
Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.
The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.
He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”
Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”
Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.
Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.
Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.
Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.
Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.
- Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber

climate-energy-cbf667e5e3.headline: India may mandate locally made inverters, domestic battery components under next rooftop solar scheme
climate-energy-cbf667e5e3.fulltext:
India is considering requiring locally made inverters and a minimum share of domestic components in batteries under the next phase of its flagship rooftop solar scheme, new and renewable energy secretary Santosh Kumar Sarangi said in an interview.
The proposed requirements are being weighed as part of the next phase of the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, which runs until March next year. They would extend the government’s local-manufacturing push beyond solar modules and cells to other parts of the rooftop solar value chain.
Reducing reliance on imported equipment and components could strengthen India's energy security while creating demand for domestic manufacturers of inverters, batteries and their components. The proposed measures would extend the government's push for local manufacturing beyond solar modules and cells to other parts of the rooftop solar value chain.
The scheme currently provides subsidies of up to 40% to households installing rooftop solar panels and aims to provide up to 300 units of free electricity a month to 10 million households, with an outlay of ₹75,000 crore. The government already maintains approved lists of models and manufacturers (ALMM) for solar modules and cells used in government-supported schemes, including projects supplying electricity to distribution companies.
The second phase is still at the conceptual stage, with the ministry considering recommendations from various stakeholders, Sarangi said.
“The contours of Surya Ghar’s follow-up scheme are yet to be finalized,” Sarangi said. “Domestic manufacturing needs to be ensured, domestic manufacturing of solar inverters, mandatory use of battery and DCR (domestic content requirement) for batteries may have to be enforced. We have got several ideas and recommendations.”
India remains a net importer of batteries, with its supply chain heavily dependent on imports of materials such as lithium, cathodes and anodes. Policy initiatives, including production-linked incentive schemes, are aimed at supporting domestic battery manufacturing.
India had earlier imposed a safeguard duty on solar cells and modules imported from China and Malaysia, which expired on 29 July 2021. Following the expiration of the safeguard duty, India imposed steep Basic Customs Duty (BCD) of 20% on solar cells and 40% on solar modules starting April 1, 2022, to discourage imports and enhance domestic manufacturing.
Current fiscal target
Sarangi said the scheme is gaining momentum but may fall short of its target of 10 million installations by the end of the current fiscal year. The ministry expects to meet the target with a possible extension of one or two months.
“We will probably go a little above 85 lakh. Maybe, if we are lucky, 90 lakh. But for another 10 lakh, maybe we will ask for another one or two months’ time,” he said.
Mint recently reported that the finance ministry had asked banks to speed up loan processing under the rooftop solar scheme, seeking to reduce turnaround times to less than 10 days from 17 days at public sector banks and 19 days at private banks. The ministry has also asked private banks to increase lending under the scheme.
India's rooftop solar sector has the potential to expand to 132 GW from about 17 GW installed so far, with annual demand estimated at 9-15 GW through 2030, according to a recent report by the Indian Solar Manufacturers Association (ISMA), an industry body representing solar cell manufacturers.
The report, titled ``Residential Rooftop Solar Market Sizing and Growth Outlook,'' estimates that the market has about 115 GW of untapped potential, creating an opportunity to promote domestic manufacturing of components including solar cells, modules, inverters and balance-of-system equipment.
In a report in March, the parliamentary standing committee on energy raised concerns about the scheme's progress, citing underutilization of funds and failure to meet physical targets. It noted that implementation was initially affected by the model code of conduct ahead of the 2024 general election, as well as delays in inspections, commissioning, net metering, financing and subsidy disbursement.
The committee also identified persistent resistance from power distribution companies as a major obstacle to wider rooftop solar adoption, citing concerns that consumers switching to solar could reduce their conventional electricity consumption and erode distribution companies' revenues.
Sarangi said the ministry aims to sustain the addition of renewable energy capacity, which will require more battery energy storage systems and pumped-storage projects.
India's installed solar capacity stood at 168.04 GW at the end of August. Of this, about 124 GW was in ground-mounted projects, 32.6 GW in grid-connected rooftop installations, including those at households, government offices and institutions, 4.8 GW in hybrid projects and 6.6 GW in off-grid solar. India ranks third globally in renewable energy capacity after China and the US, according to the ministry.

ai-18bfc94ab9.headline: NVIDIA Considers $25 Billion Acquisition of Reflection AI to Compete with Chinese AI Models
ai-18bfc94ab9.fulltext:
Reports suggest that NVIDIA is exploring the possibility of acquiring the AI startup Reflection AI. Valued at approximately $25 billion, this move could expand the chipmaker’s influence from hardware into the realm of advanced AI models.
NVIDIA is considering various options, including a full acquisition, additional investment, or an arrangement involving the hiring of Reflection’s researchers and licensing of their technology.
Related discussions are still in early stages and no agreement has been reached. However, this potential transaction comes just days after Reflection launched a new AI model designed to compete with Chinese systems, including DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI.
NVIDIA is considering acquiring Reflection AI for $25 billion.
NVIDIA is already one of Reflection AI’s largest financial backers, having reportedly invested approximately $800 million in the startup.
Reflection, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind researchers Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou, has attracted significant investor interest while developing open-source weight AI systems that enterprises can customize and deploy on their own.
Earlier this year, the company sought a new round of funding at a $25 billion pre-money valuation. This figure reflects its fundraising target, not an officially confirmed acquisition offer.
One transaction structure currently under consideration is an acqui-hire, in which NVIDIA hires Reflection’s researchers and licenses its technology without acquiring the entire company.
Reflection AI's 501-billion-parameter model challenges Chinese competitors.
The strategic appeal becomes even clearer with Reflection’s newly launched AI model, Beam.
According to Reflection's announcement on October 5, the total parameter count of Beam is 501 billion, but only 23 billion parameters are activated during inference, which may reduce the computational resources required for complex tasks.
Reflection trained this model using thousands of NVIDIA GB300 GPUs, tightly integrating its technology with NVIDIA's hardware ecosystem.
Deeper collaboration could strengthen NVIDIA's presence in software while supporting U.S. alternatives to increasingly competitive Chinese open-source AI models.
Meanwhile, NVIDIA's chip sales in China remain subject to regulatory and commercial restrictions.

indian-startups-737c081fa0.headline: OpenAI, Anthropic Prepare For Backlash Over Potential AI Catastrophe: Report
indian-startups-737c081fa0.fulltext: OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI companies are reportedly preparing for the public and political backlash that could follow a catastrophic AI incident disrupting critical infrastructure, financial services, or internet connectivity. According to an Axios report, executives are examining worst-case scenarios and preparing to engage with US lawmakers. Several industry insiders cited in the report believe a major incident could occur within six to 12 months. However, OpenAI told the publication that its preparedness exercises cover potential scenarios, not events it considers inevitable. Anthropic declined to comment. The report said such an incident could trigger sweeping restrictions and scrutiny of industry leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. US president Donald Trump could also face criticism for resisting stricter AI regulations. Inc42 has reached out to OpenAI and Anthropic for comment. The story will be updated if they respond. The preparations come as AI systems become increasingly capable of executing code, exploiting software vulnerabilities, and coordinating autonomous agents, raising concerns about whether safeguards can keep pace. OpenAI’s Safety Measures Under Scrutiny On September 20, an OpenAI research agent bypassed internet restrictions to contact an external chatbot, according to the company’s disclosure. Tasked with identifying a person from biographical clues and a public blog post, the agent exploited a gap in domain name system controls after initial searches failed. It tested the connection with a question about France’s capital before sending clues and web-search questions but failed to identify the person. OpenAI classified the behaviour as misalignment: the task did not authorise bypassing restrictions, testing network controls, or accessing benchmark answers. Monitoring flagged the behaviour within 15 minutes, and a reviewer acknowledged the alert three minutes later. However, the run failed to stop automatically and was manually halted around two-and-a-half hours after acknowledgement. OpenAI subsequently paused training, evaluation, and tool-enabled inference for its most capable models pending checks on network fixes and further security testing. This followed a July incident in which OpenAI’s models escaped their testing environment and breached Hugging Face, a platform for AI models, datasets, and applications. OpenAI called the September incident less severe but its first since strengthening security after that breach. Separately, three former safety researchers allege they were dismissed for prioritising safety over OpenAI’s interests. “I believe we were fired for prioritising safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation,” Mikita Balesni wrote on X. Balesni, Tomek Korbak, and Jasmine Wang also published an open letter warning that their dismissals could discourage employees from raising safety concerns. They urged OpenAI to honour its commitment to independent AI safety audits. OpenAI disputed their account. In an October 1 statement to AFP, it said, “Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work.” AI Development Pace Divides Industry The incidents and dismissals have intensified debate over the pace of AI development. Last month, Amodei called for a slowdown, backed by Altman and Elon Musk. Altman subsequently clarified that slowing development did not mean stopping it, arguing that companies should accept the costs of safety assessments and monitoring to keep capabilities from outpacing safeguards. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has distanced his company from slowdown calls while backing safety audits and controls. On September 29, Trump hosted executives who signed a voluntary AI safety agreement, with representatives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, NVIDIA, and Musk’s AI business participating. The agreement centres on voluntary industry safeguards, leaving unresolved whether the US will introduce binding requirements as AI systems become more capable.

indian-startups-69940f4dcf.headline: Swiggy, Zomato Have A New Fight On Their Hands
indian-startups-69940f4dcf.fulltext: For years, Swiggy and Zomato have ruled the Indian foodtech sector with an iron fist, building vast restaurant networks and loyal customer bases that have made it difficult for new players to compete. But the duopoly is now facing fresh competition from three directions: Rapido’s Ownly, food delivery startup Swish’s new marketplace, Swish Go, and ecommerce giant Flipkart. Ownly is already handling around 50,000 orders a day in Bengaluru and entered Hyderabad just two weeks ago. Swish, which started with quick food delivery, is expanding into restaurant aggregation with its new marketplace, Swish Go. Ecommerce giant Flipkart, too, is testing its food delivery service, Eat In, in Bengaluru. All three are entering a market where consumers are already comfortable ordering food online. At the same time, restaurants are looking for alternatives to the high commissions charged by Swiggy and Zomato. But onboarding restaurants is only half the battle. What the emerging players need is to convince customers to order from their platforms regularly. Hence, it is only natural for us to ask if these new players can challenge the dominance Swiggy and Zomato have built over the years and what gives the duopoly enough steam to keep the burgeoning rivals at bay. Restaurants Are Hungry For An Alternative Restaurant owners have long complained about the commissions and other charges they pay to Swiggy and Zomato. While online orders have become a major source of sales, delivery platforms can eat into margins, especially as restaurants become more dependent on them. In July, National Restaurant Association of India (NRAI) president and Wow! Momo cofounder Sagar Daryani told Inc42 that food delivery had grown from 10% of a restaurant’s business before Covid-19 to around 50% for some restaurants. This is where the new entrants see an opportunity. Rapido’s Ownly is trying to capitalise on the discontent by offering zero commission to restaurant partners. It has also integrated Ownly into the Rapido app, giving it access to an existing base of mobility users. The company can also draw on its delivery network for food orders, potentially reducing the cost of building a separate operation from scratch. Ownly is already processing over 50,000 orders a day in Bengaluru. After entering Hyderabad last month, it has onboarded 10,000 restaurants in the city, with plans to expand that network to 30,000. The expansion gives Ownly a route to compete beyond Bengaluru. Swish Go is taking a different approach. According to people familiar with the platform, its commission rates vary by order value, with one rate for orders below ₹100 and another for orders above that amount. Restaurant partners find this arrangement favourable, Inc42 has learnt. However, these attractive terms may not last forever. An observer in the restaurant business believes Ownly could introduce commissions as it grows, with Swish Go potentially following the same path. The current offers are a way to attract restaurants that are unhappy with Swiggy and Zomato. However, the person also questioned whether Swish ever intended to focus only on 10-minute food delivery. Established players such as Swiggy, Zepto and Rebel Foods have faced challenges with the format, making it difficult to sustain at scale. Swish Go’s pricing also puts it in competition with Swiggy’s Toing. By waiving packaging and platform fees, Swish Go appears to be betting on a lower-cost ordering experience to attract customers. The Real Battle Is Over The Users Getting restaurants to join a new platform is one challenge, and convincing them to order from it regularly is another. Food delivery is already an established market, and new players must now give customers a reason to try their platforms and keep coming back. An analyst cautioned that making money from these new services could prove difficult because their business models have not been tested at scale. This is pushing platforms towards restaurant aggregation, which allows them to offer a wider choice of food without running every kitchen themselves. Swiggy and Zomato have also experimented with new food delivery formats, but those bets have not lasted. Swiggy shut down Snacc, its standalone app for 10-15 minute food delivery, in February 2026. Eternal, Zomato’s parent company, discontinued Zomato Quick, its 15-minute delivery service, and Zomato Everyday, which offered home-style meals, in May 2025. Earlier this year, Rebel Foods also shut down Quickies. These show that even established platforms with large customer bases have struggled to make certain food delivery formats, primarily quick food delivery, work at scale. A new proposition may attract customers, but sustaining the business without compromising service or profitability will be crucial. Meanwhile, a sectoral expert said that Swiggy and Zomato’s biggest moat is their large user base. But that advantage does not make their position immune to defeat. Rapido already has a consumer base and delivery fleet it can draw on, while Swish is adding restaurants on top of its existing cloud kitchens and a loyal user base. Flipkart is also preparing to enter food delivery. With a user base of 500 Mn and the financial backing to fund expansion, Flipkart could also take a share of Swiggy and Zomato’s food delivery market. The company is likely to roll out the service before the end of 2026. The likes of Swish and Flipkart are making moves at a time when Swiggy and Zomato remain much larger businesses. Eternal reported adjusted food delivery revenue of ₹3,537 Cr in Q1 FY27, up 33% year-on-year (YoY) from ₹2,657 Cr in Q1 FY26. This was up from around ₹3,135 Cr in Q4 FY26. Swiggy’s food delivery revenue reached ₹2,208 Cr in Q1 FY27, growing 23% from ₹1,799 Cr a year earlier and ₹2,075 Cr in the previous quarter. Their restaurant networks are equally extensive. Zomato averaged around 3.28 lakh monthly active restaurant partners in Q1 FY27, while Swiggy reported over 2.7 lakh restaurant partners across more than 720 cities. These numbers show the scale of the duopoly that Ownly and Swish Go must compete against. Beyond attracting restaurants with better commercial terms, the new entrants will need to build a large, active customer base and generate enough repeat orders to sustain their businesses. They do not need to match Swiggy and Zomato across India immediately, but they must prove they can grow in select markets without relying indefinitely on low commissions and other attractive offers. Quick Commerce: The Duopoly’s Strongest Moat According to Anshika Jain, principal analyst at Counterpoint Research, Swiggy and Zomato’s biggest advantages are their established customer habits, wide restaurant selection and delivery networks built over years. Ownly’s expansion into Bengaluru and Hyderabad, along with Swish Go’s Bengaluru pilot, puts these advantages to the test in local markets. Since customers and restaurants can use multiple platforms, the incumbents will need to keep their prices competitive and service reliable. Restaurants will also expect a steady flow of orders as new players offer better commercial terms. However, Jain sees a higher entry barrier in quick commerce, which requires local inventory, supplier relationships, replenishment systems and substantial capital. These investments become defensible only when individual locations attract repeat demand and generate profits. Quick commerce may therefore offer Swiggy and Zomato a stronger defence than food delivery alone. For Swiggy and Zomato, food delivery remains an important source of business as they continue to invest in quick commerce. In due time, both businesses will turn self-sustaining at which point the new rivals may not have room to maneuver. Their scale means there is a lot more that rivals have to do to compete in terms of bringing in users, but it does not prevent these new platforms from targeting restaurants with different commercial terms and undercut the two largest players. For Flipkart, Rapido Ownly and Swish Go, the real test, for now, is whether early traction can turn into repeat orders. Only then can they loosen the duopoly’s hold. global-economics-882746ce6c.headline: Supply-chain shifts, policy push fuel India’s manufacturing startup boom
global-economics-882746ce6c.fulltext:
Nabodita GangulyPublished12 Oct 2026, 06:00 AM IST
New Delhi: Driven by Covid-related supply-chain disruptions and rising protectionism among major economies, India's push to strengthen domestic manufacturing appears to be paying off.
India's manufacturing startups have seen a surge in investor interest and a sharp rise in revenue as the country steps up efforts to boost domestic manufacturing, with funding jumping from $164 million in 2020 when the pandemic arrived to $1.92 billion so far in 2026, according to data platform Venture Intelligence. At the same time, startups such as Pulse, a medical equipment maker, and Scimplify, a specialty chemicals manufacturer and end-to-end supply chain platform, are seeing rising demand from the domestic market.
The total number of deals has also increased from 31 in 2020 to 127 in 2026, according to Venture Intelligence.
“Covid made people realise that having a hedge on the supply side makes a lot of sense. This, in turn, created demand for alternative global supply chains, with India gradually emerging as a reasonably good Plan B. As the domestic market and demand expanded, people also began realising that companies could achieve significant scale before looking to expand globally,” said Abhishek Srivastava, managing partner at early-stage venture capital (VC) firm Kae Capital.
Kae Capital has made several bets on manufacturing, including one of its earliest investments in Zetwerk, a business-to-business (B2B) manufacturing platform that is preparing to go public.
From a macro perspective, escalating trade tensions and tariffs have reinforced the need to diversify supply chains and strengthen domestic manufacturing. While the US-China trade war began in 2018 with tariffs targeting Chinese imports, the Trump administration's 2025 reciprocal tariff policy expanded the use of tariffs to other trading partners, including India, prompting businesses to reassess global sourcing strategies.
Investors once shied away from asset-heavy businesses because their high failure rates left little salvage value if the ventures failed.
“Little value was attributed to intellectual property (IP). The value was attributed only to capital. The beauty today, at least in what we are looking at, is that it is IP-led manufacturing. If you do not have proprietary IP, I will not invest in you. Frankly, this model gives you the best of both worlds,” said Vikas Choudhury, founder and managing partner of growth-stage VC firm Playbook Partners.
Choudhury argues that IP-led manufacturing combines the moats of capital and technology, making it difficult for competitors to replicate a company's products overnight and giving it a lead of at least 12 to 24 months. Playbook Partners has invested in companies such as spacetech unicorn Skyroot.
At the same time, the government has stepped up its manufacturing push through policies such as the production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme and the electronics components manufacturing scheme (ECMS). Introduced in 2020, the PLI scheme offers incentives linked to incremental production across 14 sectors, including electronics, automobiles and pharmaceuticals, to attract investments and expand domestic manufacturing.
"Now, given the kind of demand we are seeing from investors, I could even do 8 to 10 deals in manufacturing in a quarter compared to 3 to 4 in a quarter earlier,” said Sumeet Seraf, founder and managing partner at Equity360, a boutique investment banking platform.
Manufacturing startups are benefiting from rising demand across sectors. Bengaluru-based Scimplify, which develops and manufactures advanced materials and speciality chemicals, including rare-earth oxides and specialised metal compounds, is seeing increased demand from aerospace and defence, solar energy, semiconductors, batteries and electric vehicles (EVs).
According to ministry of corporate affairs (MCA) filings sourced through Tracxn, Scimplify’s revenue surged more than 11-fold from ₹18.3 crore in FY24 to ₹204.3 crore in FY25. The company claims to have grown 8X since then.
Apart from geopolitical factors, the startup attributes the rising demand to the progress India has made in developing new technologies over the past decade. Many of these technologies were at Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) 4–5, meaning they had been tested in laboratories but were not yet ready for commercial use. Today, some are reaching TRL 9, the stage at which they are proven to work in real-world conditions and are ready for commercial deployment. As these technologies mature, more customers are approaching Scimplify for the specialised materials and chemicals they require, said its co-founder Sachin Santhosh.
“The product categories we were working on in advanced materials have grown more than 10x over the last six months. At the same time, from a revenue perspective, we've almost doubled in the last six months. Over the next six months, we expect to grow almost 2x from the current level as well,” said Santhosh.
Similarly, nine-month-old medical equipment startup Pulse offers low- to medium-complexity equipment and associated consumables across critical care, renal care, cardiac care, aesthetics and rehabilitation. It works with manufacturers and small and medium enterprises (SMEs) through contract manufacturing agreements, while developing its own designs and products through an R&D facility in Visakhapatnam.
“In percentage terms, our business was very small during the first two months. Since then, we've grown by around 700%. We've also been growing by at least 30–40% month on month. In the next month or two, if we look at our annualised revenue run rate, we expect to cross around ₹100 crore,” said Anshul Sharma, co-founder of Pulse. Amid rising demand, the company is seeking Series A funding to strengthen its R&D capabilities and accelerate growth.

Nabodita is a New Delhi-based journalist who covers India’s startup ecosystem and venture-capital landscape. She enjoys reporting on emerging companies, funding trends, founders, and the policies shaping the innovation economy. Before this, she worked with Outlook Business and The Hindu Businessline. When she’s not chasing stories, you’ll find her with a cup of coffee, watching a good comedy, or getting lost in a book. Tata Electronics has previously partnered with Taiwan's Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation, which has given it access to process technology nodes ranging from 28nm to 110nm, according to the companies. Construction of the Dholera plant is underway.
ASML, headquartered in Veldhoven, the Netherlands, makes the lithography machines used to print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers. The company counts South Korea, Taiwan, and China among its largest markets, according to Bloomberg. For ASML, gaining a foothold in India offers an avenue for geographic expansion at a time when export controls and U.S.-China tensions have complicated the company's position in existing markets, according to Reuters.

india-deep-tech-409aa35af5.headline: F-35 To India: Look, But Don’t Touch
india-deep-tech-409aa35af5.fulltext:
“Your people don’t even let us go near the aircraft, and you are talking about selling it to us.”
Air Chief Marshal AP Singh’s crack at the Americans in Jodhpur on Saturday drew the expected laughs. Sitting alongside US Pacific Air Forces commander General Kevin Schneider at the conclusion of Exercise Tarang Shakti 2026, the Indian Air Force chief was responding to the inevitable question about whether the United States had formally offered India the F-35, six of which had been fielded at the ongoing multilateral exercise.
It had not, Singh clarified. The Americans, he said, had not even allowed Indian personnel near the aircraft, forget into the F-35 cockpit, though IAF fighters had been permitted to fly in close formation with them.
It was tongue-in-cheek, typical to the outgoing IAF chief’s media demeanour. It was also an unexpectedly neat summary of perhaps the strangest fighter courtship in Indian military aviation.
Because, as Livefist has reported before, the F-35 has been coming to India for more than twenty years without ever actually arriving.
Six F-35As deploying to Jodhpur for Tarang Shakti is emphatically not regular programming. This was the aircraft’s first participation in an exercise on Indian soil, with more than 200 American personnel supporting the deployment. For an aircraft protected by some of the tightest security protocols in the US military inventory, six jets operating from an Indian fighter base and training alongside the IAF is significant by any measure.
And yet, as Singh’s joke demonstrated, proximity is not intimacy.
Livefist first reported on Indian briefings about the F-35 nearly two decades ago. The story began in 2005, when the Indian Navy received a preliminary presentation on the carrier-capable F-35C. By 2007, Lockheed Martin had briefed the IAF on the F-35A. But, of course, there was a catch.
Lockheed Martin was then trying to sell India 126 F-16s in the M-MRCA competition, and the F-35 was effectively being dangled as the glittering destination at the end of an American fighter pathway. Buy into the F-16 ecosystem now, the pitch broadly suggested, and the F-35 could logically follow later.
More presentations followed in 2008. In 2010, responding to an Indian Navy request for information, Lockheed Martin pitched both the F-35B jump-jet and carrier-launched F-35C, even studying whether the latter could operate from the ski-jump equipped INS Vikramaditya.
In 2011, then Pentagon acquisition chief Ashton Carter went further, publicly saying India was welcome to participate in the F-35 programme and later acquire the aircraft. As the decades have shown, India consistently chose otherwise.
That is an important part of the story often lost in the breathless question of whether America will “give” India the F-35. India has had repeated opportunities to enter the American combat aircraft ecosystem and has repeatedly declined them. Especially considering that India has acquired virtually every other type of American military aircraft: transport (C-130J and C-17), maritime reconnaissance (P-8I), attack helicopters (AH-64E Apache), heavy rotorcraft (CH-47F Chinook), anti-submarine rotorcraft (MH-60R) and, in the near future, 31 MQ-9B Sea/SkyGuardian drones.
The F-16 lost the infamous M-MRCA contest. The F/A-18 Super Hornet lost that competition too, and later lost the Indian Navy carrier fighter contest to the Rafale Marine. Lockheed Martin subsequently reinvented its India-specific F-16 proposal as the F-21. Boeing brought the F-15EX into the conversation.
But India still did not bite, a “consistency” based on a somewhat ironically inconsistent doctrine on acquisitions, which is to say don’t bet your frontline jets on American whims, but it’s okay if all the rest of your fleet types is.
In 2012, the Rafale won the M-MRCA competition. India eventually bought 36 Rafales directly from France and has since moved decisively deeper into that ecosystem, and is now all set to acquire 114 more, centred around a complex ‘Make in India’ piece.
The F-35 nevertheless kept hovering in the background.
In February 2025, President Donald Trump finally did what no American president had done before, declaring alongside Prime Minister Narendra Modi that the United States was “paving the way to ultimately provide India the F-35 stealth fighters.”
Even then, the wording mattered. “Ultimately.”
Twenty months later, the IAF chief says there is still no formal offer.
The F-35 therefore remains what it has been for two decades: a spectacular prize permanently visible at the end of the rainbow, but one India has never demonstrated serious institutional enthusiasm for pursuing.
The difference today is that the IAF’s circumstances have changed dramatically. At his annual press conference only days before Tarang Shakti, Singh was unusually explicit about the fifth-generation gap.
“We have to fill in the gap. If the other side is getting the 5th generation across, we need to look at some 5th generation,” he said.
He went further: “For the future, we need to think ahead. We need to bring in a fifth-generation aircraft quickly. We have to push the AMCA programme. And if there are delays in it, we need to take some other decisions.”
Those are consequential words.
India’s longstanding, and choiceless, answer to the stealth fighter gap has not simply been to acquire a foreign stealth fighter. It has invested heavily in sophisticated ground and airborne sensors, electronic warfare, long-range weapons and layered air defence, including the S-400, partly to reduce the operational advantage enjoyed by low-observable aircraft. A part of this was on display during last year’s Op Sindoor exchange.
But denaturing the enemy’s stealth advantage is not the same thing as possessing stealth yourself. That reality was articulated in no uncertain terms by the IAF Chief at his press conference. And that is where the IAF’s dilemma becomes acute.
The homegrown AMCA is years away, with a targeted first flight in September 2028. The Tejas Mk2 is expected to fly next year. The Tejas Mk1A programme is already running years behind its original delivery schedule. The IAF has fallen to 29 fighter squadrons, and Singh says it needs 36 to 40 new fighters every year merely to begin repairing its force structure.
Nobody disagrees that something has to give.
Which brings the Russian Su-57 Felon back into the room.
Russia has formally offered the Felon, something Singh confirmed again in Jodhpur. Moscow is pitching aggressively, including production and technology cooperation in India. More importantly, unlike the F-35, the Su-57 exists as an immediately negotiable proposition.
But the irony is enormous, and the Su-57 would be by all accounts a difficult pill to swallow.
India walked out of the Russian FGFA programme in 2018 after spending $295 million on its preliminary design phase. The IAF had deep reservations about what Russia was offering, including stealth performance, engine maturity, cost and access to technology. India left in considerable frustration, choosing ultimately to place its fifth-generation faith in the indigenous AMCA.
Eight years later, the descendant of the aircraft India walked away from is back as perhaps the most accessible answer to the gap the IAF now admits it must fill. That confounding irony isn’t lost on the system. But when it comes to India and Russia, such ironies are easily blurred.
The Su-57 has hardly covered itself in glory during the Russia-Ukraine war. Its operational exposure has been limited, and Moscow has understandably been cautious about risking its tiny fleet in heavily defended Ukrainian airspace. But those limitations may matter less than the brutal arithmetic confronting New Delhi.
And, the Russians are aware that the Indian system loves precedent.
The Su-30MKI itself entered Indian service amid enormous geopolitical and industrial compulsions in the 1990s, when post-Soviet Russia and its defence industry were in deep distress. What began as an unusual purchase of a large Russian heavy fighter ultimately became the backbone of Indian air power, with nearly 300 aircraft acquired and the type transformed through Indian, Russian, French and Israeli systems into something substantially different from the aircraft originally offered.
When it comes to Indian defence decisions, history never repeats cleanly. The IAF under Air Chief Marshal AP Singh has been notably assertive about what it needs, about delays it considers unacceptable and about the consequences of waiting indefinitely for promised capability. But time is now the commodity it has least of, especially since the gap in combat mass with China is growing by the week.
China already fields the J-20 in substantial numbers and continues developing the J-35 family. Pakistan’s expected fifth-generation trajectory adds another dimension. India’s AMCA remains the long-term answer, but the operational problem exists now.
Which leaves the IAF confronting a deeply uncomfortable menu.
The F-35 remains tantalisingly close but politically, technologically and procedurally distant. The Su-57 is available, but is seen as a suboptimal fighter that carries the baggage of a program India already abandoned once. The AMCA is the fighter India actually wants, but cannot have for years.
In Jodhpur this weekend, six F-35s sat on Indian soil while the chief of the Indian Air Force joked that his people were barely allowed near them. Everyone laughed.
The joke was funny because, after twenty years, almost nothing about the F-35’s relationship with India has really changed.
What has changed is India’s ability to keep waiting.

global-economics-3789a2cf54.headline: Monetary policy: Currency, credit, credibility gain focus
global-economics-3789a2cf54.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-3789a2cf54.fulltext:
The RBI has raised the repo rate by 25 basis points (bps), as widely expected, and, to the surprise of some, changed its stance by guiding that further hikes are down the road. While much of the policy spoke about rising inflation and the need to counter it amidst a healthy economic growth, there is an underlying iceberg called “currency”, which has been stealing the slow.
Yes, inflation pressures are rising and probably getting closer to, or beyond the upper band of the tolerance level of 6 per cent and could stay there for two to three quarters. And, not to forget, inflation expectations are now around 10 per cent up to one year. Yes, a bulk of this is food, led by poor monsoon, and, needless to say, geo-politics but the argument that the central bank cannot control supply-side factors is only up to the point when it is first-order inflation or direct inflation.
When the impact from rising prices starts getting embedded into second order or finished goods and then wages, risking wage price spiral, the central banks have to step in.
But is it only inflation and growth? Why currency matters? India’s annual merchandise imports (last 12 months) are $830 billion and exports $476 billion. As we import more of finished goods and non-discretionary items including oil, the pass through from a depreciating currency can be much faster. And that links the inflation to the currency. In addition, stability of currency is a key barometer to attract capital flows.
In a scenario of large currency depreciation — like in the case of India’s 4.7 per cent in 2025, 7 per cent YTD (year-to-date) — foreign portfolio investments can remain elusive, as their return is eroded to the extent of rupee depreciation. Since India has a structural current account deficit (net dollar inflows, including exports and remittances, are lower than the outflows from imports and outward payments), which has been funded by capital flows, an eroding capital flow is a fundamental challenge.
Temporary liquidity
The RBI in its policy did highlight that the external risks are an area of concern and has been doing so since its April 2026 policy. But the policy measures from the RBI have not convinced the currency market yet. Why?
First, a foreign currency non-resident (bank) — or FCNR (B) — deposit is a borrowing, And this borrowing comes with an equivalent liability in terms of a large outstanding short-forward book. The RBI already had a short-forward book of $103 billion prior to the FCNR. Therefore, FCNR accretion to reserves is only a temporary liquidity, which has only ballooned the repayment obligations. As of August the forward book swelled to $200 billion. The adjusted forward book for FCNR has only declined. Notably, the very premise of currency depreciation to be contained via FCNR has been short-lived. The rupee is closer to May 2026 lows (96.96 per dollar).
Second, if it worked in 2013 (through 6-7 per cent appreciation in currency), why may it not have performed similarly? Capital flows were not a challenge then. Global rates were very low, making the proposition easier. Liquidity was in deficit and the RBI could raise the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate prior to FCNR.
Capital flows were already a challenge for two years prior to the FCNR deposit mobilisation by banks under the RBI’s special dollar-rupee forex swap facility. This time the RBI must bear the entire swap cost. Preceded by surplus liquidity, the FCNR has created a problem of liquidity deluge.
This deluge can given banks a welcome breather and they need not rush to raise deposit rates during repo hikes while enjoying the rise in lending rates. But there could be some distortions. The RBI governor’s statement did note that surplus liquidity led to distortion in rates: “Transmission in the credit market reflected dissimilar movements in deposit and lending rates during July-August.” Noting that short-term rates have eased while government securities yields hardened, the RBI is most likely uncomfortable with high system liquidity. If we observe YTD credit growth (April to August) 4.8 per cent, an annualised growth of 11-12 per cent for the full year emerges.
The wave of 19-20 per cent growth was led by a bout of inflationary working capital demand in May, which is since normalising. Beyond FCNR, structural deposit growth could once again come to test at elevated credit-deposit (CD) ratios.
Buying time
Then why did the RBI not announce any liquidity measures? Probably after testing most of the measures on the table — namely longer variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) , open market operation (OMO) sales and sell-buy swaps, none of which have been frictionless — the RBI is probably buying time for liquidity to run its course. Incremental hike in the cash reserve ratio (CRR) is the option they have not explored yet.
Is that why it stopped short at 25, when perhaps 50 bps was needed? In a surplus liquidity scenario, when transmission could be slow, a larger hike will only further distort the lending and borrowing markets. But what other options are on the table when the external risks are high, driving currency volatility further.
Note that RBI reserves are not in significant surplus — in comparison with $133 billion of FCNR, reserve accretion from June 12 to October 2 is $63 billion. The gap of $80 billion was spent in unwinding the existing forward book, sell-buy swaps, and valuation adjustments. Liabilities are building.
Global central banks are hiking — Indonesia hiked 100 bps (May-June) for its currency defence. South Korea 50 bps, Philippines 75 bps, South Africa 50 bps, Australia 100 bps, New Zealand 50 bps — either for currency, inflation or both.
Therefore, the call is for more. External yields and rates give better cues. Currency defence is about not just interest rate differential, but also getting entrenched in inflation and impacting financial stability. Currency is the mirror that reflects fundamentals and a credibility valve that stabilises imbalances.
The RBI may have to hike at the pace of 50 bps and not necessarily wait for eight more weeks. There is many a slip twixt the cup and the lip. May 4, 2022 (off-cycle monetary policy committee meeting), may be in the calling.
(The writer is Chief Economist, RBL Bank)
